title: Algoritmos criptográficos
description: Common algorithms and block cipher modes with their sizes and whether they are still acceptable.
rows: Current standard for bulk encryption (TLS, FDE, WPA2/WPA3). AES-256 for the strongest protection.
Deprecated and disallowed by NIST for new encryption. Slow and vulnerable to attacks on its small block size.
Broken: the key space can be brute-forced quickly. Never acceptable.
Biased keystream; behind the WEP and TKIP weaknesses and prohibited in TLS.
Legacy; the small block is a weakness. Its key schedule is the basis of bcrypt.
AES finalist; still considered secure but far less common than AES.
Legacy cipher from early PGP versions.
Modern AEAD option in TLS 1.3; fast on devices without AES hardware acceleration.
Security rests on factoring large numbers. Used for signatures and key transport; RSA key transport gives no forward secrecy.
256 to 521-bit curves (256-bit ECC is roughly 3072-bit RSA)
Same strength with much smaller keys; preferred for mobile, IoT, and certificates. ECDSA is the signature scheme.
Signs but cannot encrypt. Being retired in favor of ECDSA and EdDSA.
Agrees a shared secret over an untrusted channel; does not encrypt or authenticate by itself, so unauthenticated DH is open to on-path attacks.
Provides perfect forward secrecy; TLS 1.3 removed static RSA and static DH key exchange, so certificate-based handshakes always use (EC)DHE.
Practical collisions exist. Not acceptable for signatures or password storage.
Collisions demonstrated publicly in 2017; deprecated for certificates and signatures.
Current standard for integrity, signatures, and certificates.
Different internal design (Keccak sponge); an alternative to SHA-2, not a fix for a broken SHA-2.
Not broken but rarely used outside niche uses such as Bitcoin address generation.
Same size as the underlying hash (e.g., 256-bit with SHA-256)
Keyed hash proving integrity and authenticity. Shared key means no non-repudiation.
Configurable output; iterations of salted HMAC
Slows brute force by repeating HMAC many times. Used in WPA2-Personal to derive the key from the passphrase.
184-bit hash with a tunable cost factor
Blowfish-based, salted, deliberately slow. Good choice for stored passwords.
Configurable output, memory, and time cost
Memory-hard design resists GPU and ASIC cracking. Argon2id is the current recommendation for new systems.
Encrypts each block independently, so identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext and patterns leak. Never use.
Uses the cipher's block size; needs an unpredictable IV
Each block is XORed with the previous ciphertext; encryption cannot be parallelized and is vulnerable to padding-oracle attacks if poorly implemented.
Uses the cipher's block size; needs an IV
Turns a block cipher into a self-synchronizing stream cipher.
Encrypts a counter to produce a keystream; parallelizable, but reusing a nonce with the same key is catastrophic.
CTR encryption plus a Galois integrity tag (AEAD). Preferred mode in TLS 1.2/1.3.
CTR encryption plus CBC-MAC integrity; the WPA2 standard. WPA3 keeps it and adds GCMP-256 in WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit mode.
Interim WEP replacement used by original WPA; deprecated.
